title: Devarim: pass by gently (Deuteronomy 2:4–9)
hookLine: Israel must pass Edom and Moab without taking their land
last: TELL IT SO IT WON'T REPEAT.

lines: A STRONG CROWD, A MOUNTAIN COUNTRY.
cards: A huge crowd on the move, tired of the desert, and suddenly strong. Ahead of them is a mountain country with food and water to sell, and the people who live there are, the text says, afraid of them.
In plenty of old war stories, the big crowd takes what it wants. Moses remembers the order that came instead. Walk past.
Pay for your water. Don't take a single footstep of their land. It's a quiet moment in his farewell, and a strange order to give an army.

teach.b: The first neighbors are the children of Esau in Seir, the people of Edom. Moses calls them your brothers, because Esau was Jacob's twin.
God's instruction, as Moses retells it: they'll be afraid of you, so take good care of yourselves, and don't start a fight.

teach.h: NOT EVEN A FOOTSTEP OF LAND.
teach.b: I won't give you any of their land, not even enough to set the sole of your foot on, because I gave Mount Seir to Esau. Buy food from them with money, and buy water to drink.
And then a line that sounds almost like a parent: "these forty years the LORD thy God hath been with thee; thou hast lacked nothing." In other words, you don't need what's theirs. You never did.
Then Moab, the descendants of Lot, Abraham's nephew. Same rule.
Don't harass them, don't go to war, their land was given to them too. Notice what that means.
In this telling, the God who promised Israel a land also gave other peoples their lands, and expects Israel to honor the boundary even when it could be crossed easily.
Numbers remembers that Edom actually refused Israel passage, and Israel went around.
Deuteronomy doesn't dwell on the insult. It remembers the rule: their land isn't yours, and fear doesn't make it yours. In this telling, a strong people's power shows partly in what it walks past.

how: This passage is read in synagogues as part of Devarim, the first portion of Deuteronomy, and some commentators point to it as an example of the Torah recognizing the land rights of Israel's neighbors.

o: brothers: Edom, the children of Esau
words: Moses' memories of the road

games.q: inside the march — tap the pairs.
p: the children of Esau, in Seir

s: Israel is told it may take Edom's land because Edom is afraid
not even a footstep: God gave Mount Seir to Esau.
Moses calls the people of Edom brothers
Esau, Edom's ancestor, was Jacob's twin.
Israel was told to pay for water as it passed Edom
buy food with money, and buy water to drink.

games.q: you lead a strong, thirsty people past a land whose people are afraid of you. what does Moses say God commanded?
o: take the wells; they won't resist.
walk past and pay for food and water.
games.why: don't contend with them, not a footstep of their land, pay for what you eat and drink. you have lacked nothing.

practice: Think of a place where you have a little power: a younger sibling, a new hire, a conversation you could easily take over. Let the line sit with you, thou hast lacked nothing, and notice what you already have.
Then picture walking past what isn't yours, without resentment.

wordCard.voice: Devarim. Words, and in them a march where the strong side pays for its water and walks around.

orig.note: Hebrew: Esau, Jacob's twin. his children in Seir are the brothers Israel must pass gently.

carryVoice: Your line: pass by gently. Like the people passing Edom, you have lacked nothing. Until tomorrow.
